Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?
Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
Compulsory voting
Loyalty to a political party
Membership of a church
The five principles: democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life.
Democracy and The rule of law
There is no place in British society for extremism or intolerance.
Which of these does the UK offer its residents in return for respecting its values?
A right to a fair trial
A guaranteed job
Free housing
Exemption from tax
The UK offers freedom of belief and religion, freedom of speech, freedom from unfair discrimination, a right to a fair trial and a right to join in the election of a government.
Residents should respect and obey the law, respect the rights of others, treat others fairly, look after themselves and their family, and look after their area and the environment.
Respect and obey the law and Look after the area in which you live and the environment
The citizenship pledge includes a promise to observe the laws of the UK faithfully.
What TWO things do you need to become a permanent resident or citizen?
Speak and read English
Own property in the UK
Have a good understanding of life in the UK
Have a UK-born parent
You need to speak and read English and have a good understanding of life in the UK.
Speak and read English and Have a good understanding of life in the UK
B1 = ESOL Entry Level 3. The test questions are also written at ESOL Entry Level 3.

An ESOL course in English with Citizenship
A driving test
A citizenship interview
Nothing: you could not apply
The ESOL course in English with Citizenship ended with a test.
There is no fee for applying for permanent residence.
How many questions are in the Life in the UK test?
The test has 24 questions, different for each person at the session.
Welsh and Scottish Gaelic

What TWO things must you take to the test?
Identification
Your birth certificate translated
Proof of your address
A letter from your employer
Without identification and proof of address you cannot take the test.
Identification and Proof of your address
The test questions are based only on the history chapter.
If you live on the Isle of Man or in the Channel Islands, there are different arrangements for taking the test.
What is the official name of the country?
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
The British Isles
The United Kingdom of England
The official name is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Is the statement below true or false? "The Channel Islands are part of the UK."
The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies: closely linked but not part of the UK.
The Channel Islands are part of the UK.
What are the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man called?
Overseas territories
Devolved nations
Commonwealth realms
They have their own governments and are called Crown dependencies.
St Helena and The Falkland Islands
The whole of the island of Ireland is part of the UK.
Where is Stonehenge?
Dorset
Orkney
Suffolk
Stonehenge is in the English county of Wiltshire.
What is Skara Brae?
The best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe
A Roman fort on Hadrian’s Wall
An Iron Age hill fort in Dorset
An Anglo-Saxon burial site
Skara Brae on Orkney is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.
When did Britain become permanently separated from the continent?
About {#},{#} years ago
In {#} BC
Britain became separated by the Channel about 10,000 years ago.
Where can you see the Iron Age hill fort Maiden Castle?
Kent
Maiden Castle is in the English county of Dorset.
What marks the beginning of British history, according to the handbook?
The first coins minted in Britain, in the Iron Age
The building of Stonehenge
Iron Age people made the first coins in Britain, some with the names of kings. This marks the beginning of British history.
In which year did the Emperor Claudius lead a successful Roman invasion?
Julius Caesar failed in {#} BC; Claudius succeeded in AD {#}.
Why was Hadrian’s Wall built?
To keep out the Picts
To keep out the Vikings
To mark the border with Wales
To defend against the Normans
Hadrian built it to keep out the Picts, ancestors of the Scottish people.
How long did the Romans stay in Britain?
{#} years
From AD {#} to AD {#}: about {#} years.
Angles and Saxons
Sutton Hoo, in modern Suffolk.
Who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
St Augustine led missionaries from Rome and spread Christianity in the south.
Where did St Columba found a monastery?
Lindisfarne
On the island of Iona, off the coast of what is now Scotland.
Who united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and defeated the Vikings?
Cnut
Alfred the Great.
What was the Danelaw?
An area in the east and north of England where many Vikings settled
A Viking law code
A Danish king
A Scottish kingdom
Place names there, such as Grimsby and Scunthorpe, come from Viking languages.
Is the statement below true or false? "The Norman Conquest was the last successful foreign invasion of England."
William’s 1066 invasion was the last successful foreign invasion of England.
The Norman Conquest was the last successful foreign invasion of England.
What was the Domesday Book?
A record of towns, villages, people, land and animals in England after the Norman Conquest
A religious text
The first book printed by Caxton
A book of Anglo-Saxon laws
William the Conqueror ordered it; it still exists today.
The period after the Norman Conquest until about {#}.
What did the Statute of Rhuddlan do in {#}?
Annexed Wales to the Crown of England
United England and Scotland
Limited the power of the king
Ended the Hundred Years War
King Edward I introduced it; castles such as Conwy and Caernarvon were built.
How long did the Hundred Years War actually last?
Despite its name, it lasted {#} years.
Which battle in 1415 saw Henry V’s outnumbered army defeat the French?
Agincourt
Bosworth
Waterloo
The Battle of Agincourt, during the Hundred Years War.
In which year did the Black Death come to Britain?
{#}. One third of England’s population died.
What proportion of the population of England died in the Black Death?
One third
One half
One quarter
One tenth
One third, and a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.
Which TWO were results of the Black Death?
Labour shortages and peasants demanding higher wages
More cereal crops were grown
New social classes, including the gentry
The end of feudalism in Ireland
A smaller population meant less need for cereal crops, labour shortages, higher wages, the gentry and a strong urban middle class.
Labour shortages and peasants demanding higher wages and New social classes, including the gentry
In {#}, which king was forced to agree to the Magna Carta?
King John’s noblemen forced him to agree to it.
What did the Magna Carta establish?
That even the king was subject to the law
That everyone could vote
That the Church was independent of Rome
That Parliament must meet every year
It established that the king was subject to the law and restricted his power to tax and make laws.
Knights and wealthy people from towns were elected to the Commons.
How many Houses (Estates) did the medieval Scottish Parliament have?
Three
Two
One
Four
The lords, the commons and the clergy.
How did English judges develop "common law"?
By precedence (following previous decisions) and tradition
By writing all laws down
By following Roman law
By asking the king
In Scotland, by contrast, laws were "codified" (written down).
Which word in modern English comes from Norman French?
Beauty
Apple
Cow
Summer
Park and "beauty" come from Norman French; "apple", "cow" and "summer" from Anglo-Saxon.
By which year was English the preferred language of the royal court and Parliament?
By 1400 official documents in England were written in English.
William Caxton.

St Paul’s
Westminster Cathedral
